props.title: Hollywood Boulevard

sections.content: Hollywood Boulevard (1976) epitomizes Roger Corman's New World Pictures exploitation formula - mixing dark comedy, gratuitous nudity, and meta-commentary on Hollywood's underbelly. Director Allan Arkush and Joe Dante crafted this ultra-low-budget satire by cleverly incorporating stock footage from other Corman films like Death Race 2000 (1975) and The Big Bird Cage (1972). The film follows naive Candy Wednesday (Candice Rialson) pursuing her acting dreams in sleazy 1970s Hollywood, landing roles in cheap action flicks produced by penny-pinching studios - a direct parody of Corman's own operation.

sections.content: The film sits perfectly within the 1970s wave of Hollywood self-reflection, alongside works like The Day of the Locust (1975) and Inserts (1975). But while those films took more serious approaches to Tinseltown's dark side, Hollywood Boulevard opts for broad satire and knowing winks to B-movie conventions. The movie-within-a-movie sequences deliberately showcase awful acting and cheaper-than-cheap special effects, turning the entire production into a commentary on exploitation filmmaking itself.

What makes Hollywood Boulevard particularly fascinating is how it predates later meta-commentaries on Hollywood like The Player (1992) and Get Shorty (1995). Its blend of genuine sleaze and self-aware humor created a template for future films about filmmaking's seedier side. Directors Arkush and Dante would go on to more mainstream success, but this early collaboration captures the anarchic spirit of 1970s independent cinema. SUBHEAD: The Roger Corman Factory System

sections.content: The film provides a unique window into Roger Corman's legendary low-budget production methods. Like Targets (1968) and Return of the Movie Movie (1972), it repurposes footage from earlier films to stretch its minimal budget. This practice, which Corman perfected, influenced generations of independent filmmakers. The film's behind-the-scenes portrayal of quick-and-dirty filmmaking mirrors actual production stories from New World Pictures, where future directors like James Cameron and Francis Ford Coppola got their start.
